To enclose something means to surround it completely on all sides, or to place it inside something else so that it is contained within it. Both ideas share the same heart: a boundary is created, and something ends up inside that boundary.

The word has two distinct but closely related senses. Understanding both will give you full command of this word.
Sense 1 — To surround something completely, shutting it in

When you enclose something in this sense, you create a complete boundary around it — not a partial wall, but a full, closed-off barrier. The key is completeness. Something that is enclosed has no open side; it is wrapped, ringed, or bordered on all sides.

Examples:

  • The farmer built a fence to enclose his cattle. — The fence runs all the way around, so the cattle cannot wander out.
  • The courtyard was enclosed by tall stone walls. — You cannot enter or leave except through a gate; every side is sealed.
  • Mountains enclose the valley on three sides, making it feel like a hidden world.
  • The cocoon encloses the caterpillar while it transforms.

Notice what makes "enclose" precise here: it isn't just near something or partially around it. To enclose is to fully wrap something within a boundary, separating it from the open space outside.

This sense is why you'll often hear "enclosed space" in safety contexts — an enclosed parking garage, an enclosed room with no windows, an enclosed mine shaft. These are spaces where the complete surrounding creates concerns about air quality or escape routes.
Sense 2 — To put something inside an envelope or package along with something else

This is the everyday, practical sense you will encounter constantly in letters, emails, and formal writing. When you enclose something in a letter or package, you are physically placing it inside alongside the main item — tucking it in, so to speak.

Examples:

  • I am enclosing a copy of my resume with this application. — The resume is physically inside the same envelope as the letter.
  • Please find the cheque enclosed. — A very common phrase in formal letters, meaning: "I've put the cheque inside this envelope for you."
  • She enclosed a photograph in the birthday card.
  • He enclosed the signed contract and mailed it back.

You will frequently see the phrases "please find enclosed..." or "enclosed herewith..." in formal business or official letters. These are simply polished ways of saying: "I have included the following item inside this envelope/package."

They share the exact same logic. In Sense 1, the boundary is physical and large — walls, fences, mountains forming a closed space. In Sense 2, the boundary is an envelope or package — a smaller physical container. In both cases, something is placed inside a complete boundary, separated from the outside. The word just scales up and down depending on context.
The Nuance and Feel of the Word

"Enclose" carries a quiet sense of containment — and depending on context, this containment can feel protective, restrictive, or simply organizational.

  • Protective: A mother's arms enclose her child. The hard shell encloses the seed, keeping it safe.
  • Restrictive: High prison walls enclose the inmates.
  • Organizational: An envelope encloses documents for neat, safe delivery.

The word itself is neutral — it doesn't judge whether being enclosed is good or bad. Context does that work for you.
Related Word Forms You Should Know

Enclosed (adjective) — Used to describe a space that is fully surrounded, or an item that has been included in an envelope or package.

  • It was an enclosed garden, sheltered from the wind by tall hedges. (surrounded space)
  • Please sign and return the enclosed form. (the form that is inside this envelope)

Enclosure (noun) — Has two meanings mirroring the two senses above:

  1. A surrounded, fenced-in area. The zoo built a larger enclosure for the elephants.
  2. Something included inside a letter or package. The application had two enclosures: a passport photo and a signed declaration.

Surround vs. Enclose — "Surround" is broader and doesn't always imply a complete, sealed barrier. Police can surround a building while still leaving some exits open. But a fence encloses a field because it forms a complete, unbroken boundary. Think of "enclose" as a stricter, more complete version of "surround."

Include vs. Enclose — "Include" simply means something is part of a group or set. You include an item on a list. You enclose a document in an envelope — meaning you physically place it inside a container. "Enclose" is always about physically putting something inside something else; "include" doesn't carry that physical sense.

Contain vs. Enclose — A jar contains water, but we wouldn't say the jar encloses the water. "Enclose" stresses the act of surrounding and closing off on all sides; "contain" simply means something is held inside, without necessarily emphasizing the boundary or the act of shutting in.

Confine vs. Enclose — "Confine" means to restrict something to a limited space and almost always carries a negative tone of restriction or imprisonment. "Enclose" is neutral — it simply describes the physical reality of being within a boundary, without judging it.
A Quick Mental Image to Lock This In

Picture a letter on a desk. You fold it, place it in an envelope, add a cheque and a signed form, and seal the envelope. You have just enclosed the documents — they are now inside a complete boundary. Now zoom out: the same logic applies to a garden surrounded by a fence, a valley ringed by mountains, or an animal in a zoo pen. Something is always inside a complete boundary, separated from the open world around it. That is "enclose."
